transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, the occupational health doctor down at the precinct is the one who technically sent me here. It's been a whole ordeal, to be honest. I've been on the force for thirty years, and I've always prided myself on being disciplined, you know? But lately, they've been on my case, saying I'm not eating enough to sustain the physical demands of the job, which I think is a bit of an exaggeration. I mean, sure, I've tightened up my routine, but it's just about maintaining control. Most days, I get by perfectly fine on black coffee during my shift—it keeps me sharp, keeps me alert, and I don't get that sluggish feeling you get after a heavy lunch. Then, when I get home, I might have a plain yogurt, or maybe just a few bites of grilled chicken if I really feel like I need it. But sitting down to a full, heavy meal? It just feels wrong. It feels like I'm losing my edge, like I'm letting my standards slip after working so hard to stay disciplined all these years. I just don't see why they're making such a big deal out of it when I'm still doing my job just fine.
Do you think you would be happier if you were thinner?

Well, happier? I don't know if "happier" is the right word. I mean, happiness is subjective, isn't it? For me, it's not really about walking around with a smile on my face because I dropped a pound or two. It's more about... well, it's about satisfaction, I guess. The satisfaction of knowing I have the discipline to achieve a goal. You see, when you're on the force as long as I have been, you see a lot of guys let themselves go. They hit their fifties, they get comfortable behind a desk or even in the cruiser, and suddenly they're huffing and puffing just walking up a flight of stairs. I swore I'd never be that guy. So, if I were thinner—or rather, if I keep pushing myself to stay lean—it just proves to me that I'm still in control. It proves I haven't lost my willpower. I look in the mirror, and if I see any softness, any sign that I'm slipping into that complacent, middle-aged stereotype, it just eats at me. So, yeah, maybe I would feel better, more at peace with myself, if I could just tighten things up a little more. It's just about holding the line, you know? Maintaining the standard I set for myself thirty years ago. I don't think that's about happiness, exactly, just... not letting myself fail.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Afraid? I mean... I wouldn't use the word afraid, exactly. Fear is what you feel when you're clearing a dark building and you don't know who's behind the door. But... if you're asking if it bothers me, if it gets under my skin? Yeah. Yeah, it does. It's more of a... a visceral reaction. 

Let me explain it like this. Every morning, right after I wake up, before I even have a sip of water, I step on the scale. It's just part of the routine, right? Like shaving or putting on the uniform. But if that number is up—even by a fraction, even just half a pound—it's like... it's like a physical jolt. It hits me right in the chest. It's this immediate sense of failure, this overwhelming feeling that I've completely lost control. I start running through everything I did the day before, every single thing I put in my mouth, trying to figure out where I slipped up. And the rest of the day? It's ruined. I can't focus on anything else. I'll spend the entire shift just... obsessing over it, making sure I cut back even harder. No coffee with milk, no yogurt, nothing. Just water. Because the idea of putting weight back on, of letting that number creep up and up until I'm just another out-of-shape cop... I can't stand it. It makes my skin crawl just thinking about it. I've worked too hard, for too many years, to let myself go like that. So, afraid? Maybe not afraid in the traditional sense. But I absolutely refuse to let it happen. I just can't.
Do you have a specific weight or body shape in mind that you're trying to achieve?

Well, it's not like I have a specific number written down on a piece of paper, or a picture of some fitness model taped to my bathroom mirror. It's not about trying to look like someone else, or hitting some arbitrary metric that some doctor—no offense—decided was healthy. It's more about what I see when I look at myself. And the thing is, when I look in the mirror, I don't see what the occupational health guy sees, or what my sergeant sees when they tell me I'm looking gaunt. They use words like that—gaunt, frail. I don't see that at all. 

When I stand in front of that mirror, usually right after the scale, my eyes just zero in on my stomach and my waist. That's the battleground right there. If I can pinch anything, if there's any softness, any lack of definition around the beltline... it's just unacceptable. I'll stand there, turning side to side, checking the lines, checking the firmness. And honestly, I judge my whole day by what I see in those few minutes. If I look lean enough, if my stomach is flat and tight, then I feel like I can respect myself. I feel like I've earned the right to put on the uniform and go out there and do my job. But if I don't... if I see even a hint of slackness, it just ruins me. I feel disgusted. I feel like a fraud. It's like, how can I demand respect on the streets if I can't even maintain discipline over my own body? So, it's not a specific weight, exactly. It's a standard. A standard of looking lean enough that I don't feel ashamed of the man looking back at me.
Do you think you would still restrict your food intake if you didn't have concerns about your weight?

Well, if I didn't have concerns about my weight... see, it's really hard to separate the two. It's all tied up in this whole idea of discipline I was just talking about. I mean, the whole reason I'm even sitting in this chair talking to you right now—what actually brought me in—is because the occupational health department at the precinct got involved. They pulled me in for a routine eval and the doc there started getting on my case, saying I'm not eating enough to sustain a man on active duty. They made this whole big deal out of it, acting like I'm some sort of liability to my partner. 

They wanted to know exactly what my daily routine is, and... well, most days, I just keep it to black coffee while I'm on shift. It keeps me sharp, you know? You don't want to be sluggish or weighed down when you're out on the street, especially not at my age. You need to be ready to move. So it's just the black coffee, and then... maybe, if I really feel like I need something, I'll have a plain yogurt. Then when I finally get home after a twelve-hour shift, I might have a few bites of chicken at night. Just enough protein to keep the engine running, so to speak. 

Occupational health thinks that's completely unreasonable, but if I were to sit down and eat a whole, regular, full meal... it just feels wrong. Even if I didn't care about the number on the scale or the softness around my waist, sitting down to a big plate of food just feels like I'm letting my standards slip. It feels like I'm giving in to comfort, like I'm throwing away all that mental toughness I've built up over thirty years on the force. The act of eating a full meal itself, of getting full and heavy, it just feels like complacency. Like I'm dropping my guard. And I've spent my entire career learning never to drop my guard, so... I just can't bring myself to sit down and eat like everyone else does. It's just not who I am anymore.
Do you feel like your eating habits are related to trying to achieve a certain body shape?

Well, yeah, it's definitely tied to the shape, like I was saying about the standard. It's all connected. You know, it's funny... well, not funny ha-ha, but you know what I mean. I was at the tailor a couple of weeks ago—well, actually, it wasn't even a tailor, it was just the quartermaster down at the precinct, old Sal. I've known Sal for twenty years. Anyway, I had to go in and get my uniform altered again. The thing was just hanging off me. I mean, literally hanging, like a kid wearing his dad's suit. The shoulders were sagging, the fabric was bunching up under my duty belt. Speaking of the belt, I've had to punch three new holes in the leather just to keep it from sliding down my hips. I used to be right in the middle notch, perfect fit, for years. Decades, even. And now I'm cinching it past the old notches, pulling it as tight as it'll go. 

So I'm standing there, and Sal is pinning the fabric, and he's giving me this look. You know the look. And then I go in for that occupational health eval I mentioned, and the nurse there—she's this young kid, maybe two years out of nursing school—she puts me on the scale, looks at the chart, looks at me, and tells me my weight is "dangerously low." Dangerously low. That's the exact phrase she used. She started talking about BMI and organ strain and all this medical jargon. 

And you know what I thought while she was talking? While she's standing there telling me I'm dangerously underweight and my uniform is practically swallowing me whole? I looked down at my waist, at where the belt was sitting, and I just thought... "I could stand to be a little sharper." I really did. I didn't look at the numbers she was pointing at. I just pictured myself in the mirror that morning, and I thought about how there was still that tiny bit of give when I pressed my hand against my stomach. I thought, if I just cut out the yogurt entirely, if I just push a little harder, I could finally get that perfectly clean, sharp line. So, yeah, it's about the shape. Even when they tell me I'm too small, all I can see is that I'm not sharp enough yet. It's like I can't even process the words "dangerously low" because the shape... the shape just isn't right yet.
Do you think you would consider yourself a success as a police officer if you weren't as lean as you are now?

Well, that’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? Success. You see, being a police officer—especially when you've been on the force as long as I have, over thirty years now—it’s not just a job you clock in and out of. It’s an identity. When I first joined the academy back in the day, they drilled this concept into us called "command presence." You walk into a room, a domestic dispute, a chaotic scene on the street, and people need to know instantly that you are in charge, that you have authority, and that you are completely in control of the situation. 

And how do you project that control if you don't even have control over your own physical form? So, to answer your question... no. No, I really don't think I could consider myself a success if I weren't as lean as I am now. If I let myself go, even a fraction of an inch, I’d feel like a total failure. 

It goes back to exactly what I was trying to explain to you earlier about my morning routine. When I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. The occupational health doctor, the young nurse, Sal down at the quartermaster—they look at me and see someone who is, what did they say, "dangerously low" or frail. But I look in that exact same mirror and my eyes just bypass all of that and focus entirely on my stomach and my waist. That is the ultimate measure of a man's discipline. 

I literally judge my whole day, my entire sense of worth, by whether I look lean enough right there at the beltline to respect myself. If I wake up and I look in that glass and I see a flat, hard, perfectly lean stomach, then I can put on the badge. I can go out there and be a cop. I have the right to enforce the law because I am enforcing the strictest laws on myself. But if I wasn't this lean? If I was soft? I wouldn't have any self-respect. And if I don't respect myself, the guys on the street sure as hell aren't going to respect me. I've seen guys on the force who let themselves get a gut, who sit in the cruiser eating junk all day, and they're a joke. I swore I would never, ever be that guy. So my success is entirely tied to keeping that edge, keeping that sharpness, no matter what anyone else thinks they see when they look at me.
Do you feel your self-worth would be affected by your weight if you were no longer a police officer?

Well, even if I handed in my badge and my gun tomorrow... say I just retired, packed up, and moved down to Florida like half the guys in my precinct are always talking about doing... honestly, it wouldn't change a single thing. Because it’s exactly like I was just trying to explain to you a second ago about my morning routine. 

You take away the uniform, you take away the cruiser, and I'm still the exact same guy waking up and doing the exact same thing. I could be wearing a Hawaiian shirt and flip-flops, completely off the clock for the rest of my life, but when I look in the mirror, I'm still not going to see what everyone else claims they see. I'm not going to see this frail old man that occupational health keeps lecturing me about. My eyes are still going to bypass everything else and lock right in on my stomach and my waist. 

It’s ingrained in me now. The job might have been the excuse at first, you know, the whole command presence thing I mentioned, but at this point? It’s just who I am. I would still judge my entire day, my whole sense of whether I even deserve to walk around and take up space, by whether I look lean enough right there in the midsection. If I woke up in retirement and saw any softness, I wouldn't respect myself. I just wouldn't. I'd feel like I let myself deteriorate, like I gave up. So, police officer or not, that flat, hard stomach... that's my baseline for self-worth. I don't think I could ever separate the two, not after all these years. It's just... it's how I know I'm still holding the line, even if it's just for myself.
Do you think you would still feel the need to restrict your food intake if you didn't have the fear of gaining weight?

That's... well, that's hard to even wrap my head around. If I didn't have the fear? Because the fear is... it's everything. It's the whole reason I do what I do, so trying to imagine my life without it is like trying to imagine breathing underwater. 

Let me put it this way, just to give you an idea of how deep this goes. I have this routine. Every single morning, right after I shave, before I even put on my undershirt or have a single drop of black coffee, I step on the scale in my bathroom. I actually bought a new digital one a couple of years back because the old analog one just wasn't precise enough anymore. I need to know the exact decimal, I need to see the absolute truth of where I stand before I can even start my day. 

And if I step on that scale and it is up even half a pound... I mean, literally just point-five, which I know, logically, people say is nothing, just water weight or whatever... but if I see that number go up, I get this immediate jolt. It's like a physical shock right in my chest, like a shot of adrenaline but in the worst way possible. It feels exactly like I've completely lost control. Like I took my hands off the steering wheel and the cruiser is just veering straight into oncoming traffic. 

When that happens, when I get that jolt, it dictates the next twenty-four hours of my life. I'll spend the entire rest of the day cutting back even harder than I normally do. If I had planned on having a piece of dry toast or an apple during my shift, I scrap it entirely. I'll just drink ice water, maybe chew some gum, and push myself to the absolute limit, because I just... I can't stand the idea of putting weight back on. The thought of that number climbing, of losing that edge and going backwards after I've fought so incredibly hard to get here... it honestly makes me sick to my stomach. 

So, to answer your question... no, I probably wouldn't feel the need to restrict my food like this if I wasn't terrified of gaining weight. But I am. I'm terrified of it every single time I close my eyes. That fear is the engine running the whole machine, doc. Without it, I don't even know what my day would look like, because right now, keeping that weight from coming back is my entire full-time job.
Is your decision to restrict your food intake more about avoiding weight gain or achieving a specific body shape?

Well, they kind of bleed into each other, don't they? But... if you're really forcing me to split hairs, to get right down to the brass tacks of it... I'd have to say it's the shape. It's that specific look. I know I keep coming back to this, I know I've already talked your ear off about my morning routine, but it really is the absolute center of my universe. 

The number on the scale, the weight itself—that gives me the panic, sure. But the shape... the shape is the final verdict. Like I was telling you before, when I stand in front of that bathroom mirror, I am completely blind to whatever it is the rest of the world thinks they're looking at. The department docs, the guys at the precinct, they look at my shoulders or my face and they tell me I look like a skeleton, that I'm wasting away. But I honestly don't see it. It's like my brain just edits all that out. My eyes zero in, just like a laser, right on my stomach and my waist. 

That specific shape—that tight, flat, completely lean look right at the beltline—that is the deciding factor for my entire day. I literally judge whether I am worthy of respect by the shape of my midsection. If I stand there and I see even the slightest hint of softness, or if the shape isn't exactly as hard and concave as it needs to be, the whole day is ruined before I've even put my boots on. So the restricting... yes, I'm terrified of gaining the weight, but the restricting is really the tool I use to carve out that shape. Because if I don't have that exact shape, if I don't look lean enough right there at the core, I just can't respect the man looking back at me. I'll stand there for twenty, thirty minutes sometimes, just turning side to side, checking the angles under the harsh bathroom lights, making sure the shape is perfect, because without it... I just feel like a fraud.
Is your main goal to avoid gaining weight or to achieve a specific body shape?

I know I just sort of touched on this, but to be absolutely clear... it is the shape. That's the ultimate goal. The weight on the scale is really just a number that tells me if I'm in danger of ruining the shape, you know? 

Because... well, like I was trying to explain a minute ago, when I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. It's actually kind of bizarre when you really stop and think about it. The guys at the station, my lieutenant, the occupational health docs... they'll pull me aside and say things like, 'Hey, you're looking skeletal,' or 'You're wasting away, you need to eat something.' And I just look at them like they're speaking a completely foreign language. Because when I stand in front of that glass every morning, with the bathroom light on, my eyes don't see a skeleton. I don't see my shoulders or my arms or my face. I bypass all of that completely. I focus entirely, one hundred percent, on my stomach and my waist. 

That's the battleground right there. That one specific area. And I will literally judge my whole day—my entire mood, my confidence, whether I even have the right to put on my uniform and walk out the front door—by whether I look lean enough right there at the beltline to actually respect myself. If I don't have that specific, carved-out, completely flat shape... if there's even a fraction of an inch of softness when I turn to the side, all the respect I have for myself just completely evaporates. I feel undisciplined. I feel weak. So, avoiding weight gain is the daily maintenance, sure, but the main goal, the only goal that really matters when it comes down to it, is achieving and keeping that exact shape. Because without it, I just don't know how I'm supposed to look myself in the eye.
Is your restrictive eating primarily driven by a fear of gaining weight or by a desire to maintain a specific body shape?

Doc, I... I feel a bit like I'm giving testimony on the stand and the defense attorney just keeps asking the exact same question, hoping I'll trip up or change my story. I know we are going over the exact same ground here, but I really want to make sure you understand this, because it's... well, it's the core of everything I'm dealing with. 

So, to put it as plainly as I possibly can: it is the desire to maintain that specific shape. The restricting, the fasting, the skipping meals—it's all just a means to an end, and that end is the shape of my midsection. 

Because, like I've been trying to explain, when I look in that mirror in the morning... I just don't see what everyone else says they see. My lieutenant tells me I look like hell, the guys at the precinct tell me I need to eat a steak, but I don't see this 'skeleton' they keep talking about. I just don't. My brain doesn't process it that way. I completely ignore my arms, my chest, my face... I focus entirely on my stomach and my waist. That is the sole jurisdiction that matters to me. 

And I will literally judge my whole day by whether I look lean enough right there to actually respect myself. It dictates everything. My mood, my worth, my ability to do my job. If I don't have that perfectly flat, carved-out shape at the beltline, I feel like a complete fraud putting on my uniform. I just can't respect myself if I think I'm getting soft. So yes, the fear of gaining weight is massive, it's always there, but it's only there because gaining weight means losing that shape. The shape is everything.
Do you think you could ever consider yourself healthy and respectable without maintaining your current strict eating habits and lean physique?

Could I... could I ever consider myself healthy and respectable without the strict habits and... and this physique? 

Doc, I... I honestly don't know how to even conceptualize that. I mean, my brain just hits a brick wall when I try to picture it. It's like asking me if I could still be a cop without the badge, the gun, the uniform, the training... it's just so baked into who I am at this point. 

Because, you know, I keep coming back to this, and I know I sound like a broken record, but it really all comes down to that moment in the bathroom every single morning. When I look in the mirror... I just don't see what everyone else says they see. I don't see the guy my lieutenant pulls aside to ask if he's sick. I don't see the guy the precinct docs are threatening to bench. I don't see that guy. 

I just focus... I hyper-focus, really... on my stomach and my waist. That's the entire world to me in that moment. And I judge the whole day—my entire capacity to be a respectable man, a capable officer, a person of any worth whatsoever—by whether I look lean enough right there. If I were to let go of the eating habits, if I were to just... eat like a "normal" person, whatever that means, and lose that leanness... I would lose the respect. Not just from others, but from myself. And if I can't respect myself when I look in that mirror, how am I supposed to walk out into the world and expect anyone else to respect me? How am I supposed to command a scene, or back up my partner, if I feel like a soft, undisciplined fraud underneath the uniform? So... no. No, I don't think I could. The physique, the leanness... it's the foundation of my self-respect. Without it, the whole house just caves in.
Is your restrictive eating more about achieving a specific body shape or avoiding weight gain?

Doc, I... look, with all due respect, are you reading off a checklist? Or is this some kind of standard psychiatric interrogation technique? Like asking the suspect the same question five different ways to see if the alibi holds up? Because I swear to you, we have circled this exact block multiple times now. But alright, I'll play ball. I'll keep explaining it until we're on the same page, because it's the only way I know how to make sense of it myself.

It is the shape. It has always been about the shape. The restrictive eating, skipping the mess hall, tossing out the meals... it's all just a tactical approach to getting and keeping that specific shape. 

Because—and I know I've said this, but it really is the crux of the whole thing—when I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. They see the uniform hanging off my shoulders, they see whatever it is that makes my lieutenant pull me into his office with that concerned look on his face, but I don't see any of that. I don't see a guy who's "wasting away." My brain literally does not register it. I zero in, with absolute tunnel vision, on my stomach and my waist. That's the perimeter. That's the only zone that matters. 

And I will stand there in the bathroom, at 0430 in the morning under those harsh lights, and I will judge my whole day by whether I look lean enough right there to actually respect myself. If I turn to the side and the profile isn't completely flat, if it isn't carved out exactly the way I need it to be, my self-respect just drops to absolute zero. I feel like a sloppy, undisciplined rookie who has no business carrying a badge. So the food... restricting the food is just how I make sure that when I look in that mirror, I see a waistline that allows me to put my duty belt on and actually feel like a man who deserves to wear it. Does that... does that finally clarify it for you, Doc?
Is your main motivation for restricting your food intake the fear of gaining weight or the desire to achieve a specific body shape?

Doc... seriously? Are you... are you messing with me right now? Because I feel like I'm stuck in some kind of Groundhog Day loop here. I mean, is this a test? Are you trying to see if my story changes if you ask the exact same question four different times? Because if I were interrogating a suspect and asked him the same thing this many times, his lawyer would have thrown a chair at me by now. 

Look, I'll say it again. I will keep saying it until you write it down or whatever it is you need to do to move past this, because I really need you to grasp this. It is the shape. The shape is the motivation. I don't care about the number on a scale, I care about the mirror. 

Like I have been telling you, over and over... when I look in the mirror, I just don't see what everyone else says they see. Everyone at the precinct is treating me like I'm made of glass, telling me I'm wasting away, but I just don't see it. I look in that glass, and my vision just locks onto my stomach and my waist. That is the only thing that exists in that moment. And I will literally judge my entire day—my mood, my capability, my worth as a human being—by whether I look lean enough right there to actually respect myself. 

If my stomach isn't completely flat, if I don't have that exact lean shape when I'm putting on my uniform, I despise myself. I feel sloppy. I feel weak. So the food restriction, the fasting, all of it... it's just the tool I use to maintain the shape, because that shape is the only thing keeping my self-respect intact. Please, Doc, tell me you understand this now so we can finally move on.
Is your restrictive eating habits more about achieving a certain body image or is it primarily to prevent weight gain?

Okay, look, Doc. I know I literally just sat here two minutes ago and told you I don't care about the number on the scale, but... well, you are really wearing me down with this, alright? You're asking the same thing over and over, trying to split hairs between the shape and the weight, so let me just lay the whole entire process out for you so we can finally put a pin in this. 

Yes, it's about the shape in the mirror, like I said. But how do you think I maintain that shape? They're tied together. I can't separate them. I have my routine, right? I get up at 0430, I look in the mirror, and then, yes, I step on the scale. And I'll tell you exactly what happens in my head when I do. If that scale is up even half a pound... just half a pound, Doc... I get this massive jolt. It's this physical spike of panic in my chest, like I've completely lost control of my body, my discipline, the whole operation. It feels like the steering wheel just snapped right off in my hands. 

And when that happens, when I see that number tick up even a fraction, it dictates my entire shift. I will spend the rest of the day cutting back even harder than usual. I'll skip the black coffee, I'll take the stairs up to the sixth floor at the precinct, I'll find reasons to stay out on foot patrol instead of riding in the cruiser—whatever it takes, because I absolutely cannot stand the idea of putting weight back on. Because if I put weight back on, it means I'm getting soft. It means the shape goes, the discipline goes, and I'm just another sloppy guy in a uniform. So, is it about preventing weight gain? Yes. It's all of it. The mirror, the scale, the shape, the weight—it's all one giant mechanism to keep myself in line. 

So please, tell me you've got enough notes on this now. Can we finally move on to something else?
Is your restrictive eating primarily driven by the fear of what gaining weight would do to your appearance, or by the desire to achieve a specific body shape?

Doc, I... I am actually at a loss for words right now. Are you... is your pen out of ink? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. You are asking me the exact same question for what, the fourth, the fifth time? Appearance, shape, weight—it is all the same damn thing to me! I don't know how else to explain the mechanics of my own brain to you, but I'll spell it out one last time, in as much excruciating detail as you need, since we are apparently never, ever moving past this one specific topic. 

Like I have been telling you for the last twenty minutes... when I look in the mirror, I do not see what everyone else claims they see. I just don't. My partner, the guys at the precinct, they look at me and they see this frail old guy wasting away in a uniform that's too big for him. But when I stand in front of that glass, my eyes do not process that image. It's like my brain completely filters out the rest of my body and just zeroes in, with this sick, intense laser focus, right on my stomach and my waist. That's it. That is the entire battleground. 

And I will stand there, analyzing every shadow, every angle, and I will judge my entire day—my mood, my worth, my right to even put on my badge—by whether I look lean enough right there to actually respect myself. If there is even a hint of softness, if it isn't perfectly flat and rigid, I feel like a complete disgrace. I feel undisciplined. I feel like a fraud. So call it shape, call it appearance, call it weight, call it whatever you need to check off the little box on your clipboard, Doc. It’s about looking in that glass and seeing a man I don't absolutely despise. 

Now, please, for the love of God, tell me you wrote that down so we can talk about literally anything else.
Is your restrictive eating habit more about fearing the consequences of weight gain or achieving a specific body image?

Doc... I... I'm actually starting to think this is a joke. Are you recording this? Is there a hidden camera in here? Because I swear to God, you have asked me this exact same question, in slightly different words, five times now. Five times! I feel like I'm taking a polygraph and you're just waiting for me to slip up on a detail. 

I don't know how many different ways I can explain the mechanics of my morning routine to you, but fine. Fine. I will walk you through it again, step by excruciating step, because clearly, my previous explanations haven't made it onto your notepad. 

You want to know about the fear of weight gain? Yes. Yes, it's there. It's... it's the whole foundation of the thing. Like I told you before, I get up at 0430, right? Every single morning. The alarm goes off, my feet hit the floor, and the very first thing I do, before I even turn on the shower, before I even think about making coffee, is step on that scale. And I'm telling you, Doc, the tension in my chest while I wait for those digital numbers to settle... it's like waiting to hear if a suspect has a weapon drawn behind a door. 

If that number is exactly where I want it, or lower, I can breathe. I can go about my day. But... but if that scale is up... and I'm not talking about five pounds, Doc. I'm talking about half a pound. If it is up even half a pound, I get this massive, physical jolt. It's like a shot of pure adrenaline, but not the good kind. It's this spike of sheer panic right in the center of my chest, because it feels like I've completely lost control. It feels like the discipline, the routine, the entire operation I've built to keep myself functioning has just completely fallen apart.
